title: Are cognitive-behavioral treatments effective for anxiety?

readings.title: Source 1: CBT for social anxiety disorder
readings.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether a 12-week course of cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) reduces symptoms of social anxiety disorder.

Participants

80 adults ages 18 to 45 with social anxiety disorder, diagnosed by a clinician, were recruited through a university clinic in England. All gave written informed consent; those on the waitlist were offered CBT when the study ended.

Method

Participants were randomly assigned to 12 weekly CBT sessions (testing fearful thoughts and gradually facing feared social situations) or to a 12-week waitlist. Symptoms were measured before and after with a 24-item social anxiety scale (0 to 100; higher scores mean more severe symptoms).

Results

Mean scores fell from 62 to 38 in the CBT group and from 61 to 57 in the waitlist group. The difference between the groups after 12 weeks was statistically significant.

Discussion

CBT reduced social anxiety far more than waiting for treatment.

Invented study for practice.

readings.title: Source 2: CBT, medication and a placebo pill for panic disorder
readings.html:
Introduction

Researchers compared CBT with an antidepressant medication for panic disorder, during treatment and after it ended.

Participants

150 adults ages 20 to 60 with panic disorder were recruited at four US medical centers. All gave informed consent and could leave at any time; an institutional review board approved the study.

Method

Participants were randomly assigned to 12 weeks of CBT, an SSRI antidepressant, or a placebo pill. Neither the participants given pills nor the doctors knew who received the SSRI. A "responder" had at least a 50% drop in panic symptoms. Responders were followed for six months after treatment stopped to see who relapsed (had symptoms return).

Results

At 12 weeks, 58% of the CBT group, 56% of the SSRI group and 30% of the placebo group were responders. Six months after treatment ended, 12% of CBT responders and 35% of SSRI responders had relapsed.

Discussion

CBT and medication worked about equally well during treatment, but gains after CBT lasted longer.

Invented study for practice.

readings.title: Source 3: One-session exposure for children's dog phobia
readings.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether a single three-hour session of gradual exposure, a behavioral part of CBT, helps children with a specific phobia of dogs.

Participants

40 children ages 8 to 12 with a specific phobia of dogs were recruited through pediatric clinics in Sweden. Parents gave written consent and each child gave assent; children could stop the session whenever they wished.

Method

Children were randomly assigned to one three-hour session of gradual exposure with a calm, trained dog, or to a three-hour session of education about dogs with no contact. One week later, each child walked toward a calm, leashed dog; the researchers recorded whether the child could stand next to the dog for 30 seconds.

Results

14 of the 20 children (70%) in the exposure group stood next to the dog for 30 seconds, compared with 5 of the 20 (25%) in the education group.

Discussion

A single session of exposure helped most children approach the feared animal.

Invented study for practice.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.

rubric.point: Proposes a defensible claim that answers whether cognitive-behavioral treatments are effective for anxiety.
accept: Cognitive-behavioral treatments are effective for anxiety disorders.
CBT reduces anxiety symptoms, and its gains last longer than those of medication.

parts.sample: Cognitive-behavioral treatments are effective for anxiety disorders: they reduce symptoms much more than waiting, about as much as medication during treatment, and their gains last longer.

parts.label: B(i)
parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.

rubric.point: Cites one source and states a specific, accurate result from it that supports the claim (not a method or participant detail).
accept: In Source 1, social anxiety scores fell from 62 to 38 with CBT but only from 61 to 57 on the waitlist.
According to Source 3, 70% of children given exposure stood next to the dog, compared with 25% given education.

parts.sample: According to Source 1, adults with social anxiety disorder who had 12 weeks of CBT saw their mean social anxiety score fall from 62 to 38, while the waitlist group only fell from 61 to 57.

parts.label: B(ii)
parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from B(i) supports your claim, using a psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding learned in AP® Psychology.

rubric.point: Explains how the evidence supports the claim.
accept: The CBT group improved by 24 points against 4 for the waitlist, so the treatment, not time alone, reduced symptoms.

rubric.point: Applies a psychological concept (not a restricted term) to the evidence and links it to the claim.
accept: cognitive restructuring of fearful thoughts about being judged
exposure therapy: repeatedly facing feared social situations

parts.sample: The CBT group dropped 24 points while the waitlist dropped only 4, so the treatment, not just the passing of time, reduced symptoms. In CBT, participants used cognitive restructuring: they tested thoughts such as "everyone will see I am nervous and think I am stupid" and replaced them with more accurate ones. Less distorted thinking about being judged would lower fear in social situations, which is why Source 1 supports the claim that cognitive-behavioral treatment is effective for anxiety.

parts.label: C(i)
parts.prompt: Support your claim using a different piece of specific and relevant evidence from another source.

rubric.point: Cites a different source from B(i) and states a specific, accurate result that supports the claim.
accept: In Source 3, 70% of children in the exposure group stood next to the dog, compared with 25% in the education group.
Source 2 found that only 12% of CBT responders relapsed, compared with 35% of SSRI responders.

parts.sample: In Source 3, 70% of children with a dog phobia who had one session of gradual exposure could stand next to a calm dog for 30 seconds a week later, compared with only 25% of children who had an education session.

parts.label: C(ii)
parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from C(i) supports your claim, using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding from the one in B(ii).

rubric.point: Explains how the evidence supports the claim.
accept: Contact with the dog, not information alone, made the difference.

rubric.point: Applies a different psychological concept from B(ii) and links it to the evidence and the claim.
accept: extinction: the dog (conditioned stimulus) appeared again and again without harm
habituation: with each safe contact with the calm dog, the fear response weakened

parts.sample: The education group learned the same facts about dogs but had no contact, so the contact made the difference. In exposure, the dog, a conditioned stimulus for fear, appeared again and again without anything bad happening, which leads to extinction of the conditioned fear response. Because extinction weakened the fear, most children could approach the dog, which shows that this behavioral part of cognitive-behavioral treatment is effective for anxiety.
